speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PEACE KEEPING-PARTICIPATION WHEN ENTIRE COST BORNE BY CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the negative decision by the UN in respect of the Canadian resolution which was designed to establish a satisfactory basis for financing the peacekeeping operations, is the Canadian government considering any change in its policy of participation in operations where the entire cost of maintaining its forces must be borne by Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secrelary of Slale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PEACE KEEPING-PARTICIPATION WHEN ENTIRE COST BORNE BY CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wished to make sure that I understood my hon. friend's question. There is no United Nations force, in which Canada is participating, where the full cost of our forces is borne by Canada. In the case of Cyprus we bear some of our own maintenance costs, but certain other costs are paid by the United Nations. In any event the disposition of our resolution-not a negative result in the sense that it has been defeated, it has simply been put over to the resumed session-does not in any way involve a change of policy on behalf of the government of Canada. We continue to believe that peace keeping is an important function of the United Nations, and we continue to believe that we must strive for an equitable way of financing future United Nations peace keeping operations.

subtopic: PEACE KEEPING-PARTICIPATION WHEN ENTIRE COST BORNE BY CANADA
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question I should like to direct to the Minister of National Defence. In view of the disinterest in, and indeed hostility to, the expansion of the peace keeping capabilities of the United Nations as exhibited yesterday by
Inquiries of the Ministry the disastrous defeat of the Canadian resolution in the general assembly, will the minister now give serious consideration to revising his plan for a single unified service?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: PEACE KEEPING-PARTICIPATION WHEN ENTIRE COST BORNE BY CANADA
speechtext:
Most certainly not, Mr. Speaker. When the white paper was written in 1964 it was decided on the basis of our experience that the best way we could contribute to future peace keeping operations, if and when they were authorized by the United Nations and the government of Canada, was by developing a well trained and well equipped mobile conventional force. That is the policy that was laid down in the white paper and it was the policy of the government. It is still the policy of the government and the armed forces. The forces we are developing are precisely those which can make a maximum contribution, not just to the deterrence of war in Europe or the central front, but anywhere else they are required for peace keeping operations whenever the need arises.
Therefore, my hon. friend should take some comfort from the fact that we are able to contribute whenever and wherever we are required to do so. The forces we are developing will give us the flexibility to carry out our obligations.
Bight Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, is not the entire statement of the minister purely theoretical in view of the fact that the government suffered a major diplomatic set-back in the defeat of the Canadian resolution.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, I have only a few comments to make on this particular clause of the old age security legislation.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) did not provide a satisfactory answer yesterday concerning the question of provinces which might want to implement or take over the old age security program.
The minister's defence is that this is merely hypothetical. Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the minister that it is more than a hypothetical question since it was specifically referred to in the speech from the throne, delivered at the opening of the present session of the Quebec legislature: That means that the government of Quebec firmly intends to take over the old age security field, since it announced it in the speech from the throne. Consequently, when he asks us to pass this bill, I feel it is the minister's duty to inform us as to the position he will take when the Quebec government decides to implement its own old age security program.
The minister must not ignore a situation which, obviously, is about to occur, since, as I said earlier, it is mentioned in the speech from the throne. The minister must not, like the ostrich, hide his head in the sand; on the contary, he should know what action will then be required. That is why we want an answer from the minister, since the speech from the throne clearly indicates that Quebec intends to recover control over the field of old age security. Faced with such a situation, what will the minister do? Why not provide, in the present legislation, for a fiscal compension to be paid to the provinces-or to Quebec, if that were the case for that province-which would decide to take over the control and administration of old age security?
I feel the Minister of National Health and Welfare should give us an answer in that connection. As a matter of fact, he should even provide in this bill for a fiscal compensation that would reduce or remove the problem raised by section 94A of the B.N.A. Act which grants priority rights to the provinces in the field of old age security.
I therefore ask the minister to tell us plainly what he will do when Quebec has passed the piece of legislation announced in the 23033-7191
Old Age Security Act Amendment speech from the throne. I also ask him whether he does not intend, at this stage, in view of what will happen, to amend the bill so as to provide for a fiscal compensation to be paid to any province that wants to establish its own old age security plan.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, now that the Prime Minister is present opportunity should be taken to let the house and the country know what is the attitude of the government with reference to a situation that will shortly arise when the legislature of Quebec implements legislation to exercise its jurisdiction in reference to old age security and old pensions in general? We have been endeavouring to secure information about that on two or three occasions.
Is it the intention of the government of Canada, in pursuance of its avowed dedication to unity to assure a province that in the event the province utilizes the power it has, the federal government, by subsidies and the like, will make available the necessary money to the province when it withdraws from the national plan? That is not a suggestion on my part in any way. It is simply a question as to what is going to be done. We have endeavoured to secure information from the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but the information has been as arid as the Sahara. We have not been able to get anything.
This surprises me, because I recall so well the various steps taken by the Prime Minister in his vocal adhesion to co-operative federalism. Is it now the intention of the government to desert its declaration in favour of that principle, or does it intend to apply it in such a way that, in a manner similar to that provided for in health insurance, the province or provinces can adopt a duality of system within this country? Where any province takes unto itself the enactment of legislation within its jurisdiction, the federal parliament has correlative jurisdiction, as provided by section 94A of the B.N.A. Act.

Mr. Chairman, the right hon. gentleman has complained that he has not been able to get any information from this side on the constitutional point which he has brought up. But I would remind him that he got a statement last night from the Minister of National Health and Welfare, which I think dealt quite clearly and conclusively with this question. I have little to add to that statement.

Naturally, we believe we have complete constitutional authority to introduce this legislation, just as the federal government had authority to introduce pensions legislation in the first place. I recall that after that legislation was introduced there were many occasions in Quebec when the right of the provincial government was reserved to introduce legislation of this kind under the constitution, if they saw fit, because they do have the right to do it also. But there is no doubt in our mind of our constitutional jurisdiction in this field. We are exercising it now, Mr. Chairman, as it was exercised in the past. Indeed, as my right hon. friend himself was going to exercise it when he moved an amendment to this bill adding $25 to the pension.

The right hon. gentleman said that a situation will shortly arise in Quebec by which we will be confronted with a particular piece of legislation. Mr. Chairman, he bases that statement on an intention in a speech from the throne in a provincial legislature. We do not know when that intention will be implemented. We do not know in what terms it will be implemented, if it ever is implemented, so to postpone action in this house in a matter of this kind because of that hypothetical situation would, I think, be entirely irresponsible.

I never at any time suggested its postponement. If the Prime Minister laughs, I would ask where in the statement I made did I infer that there should be a postponement? I know that this government placed a lot of stuff in several speeches from the throne. They regard that as simply decoration. But I believe when the province of Quebec today places anything in the throne speech, it means to bring in the legislation and depart from the lack of principle that has been characteristic of this government.

speechtext: I am convinced that the government of Quebec has a capacity for integrity in carrying out its pledges which has never been characteristic of this government. Until I find the contrary, I must accept that. Now then, I say to the Prime Minister, why all this evasive by-play? Nobody is objecting to the legislation which is before the house. What we are asking is this: What is going to happen to your highly vaunted co-operative federalism which you marched forth on every occasion in the past and ran away from whenever you were faced with reality? What are you going to do? The answer of the Prime Minister is one of complete evasiveness. He refuses to answer the question because he seems to believe that when the federal parliament passes this legislation it will then have exclusively occupied the field of old age security pensions and that from that day on the provinces will have no authority. That is not my reading of section 94A.

That is fine; the interruptions of hon. gentlemen opposite, as in so many cases, represent the complete contribution that they make to debate in this house. The only thing I regret is that they cannot be recognized individually by Hansard by their oh's and ah's, so that at least among their constituents they would be given credit for these interruptions.
What is obvious is that the Prime Minister will not answer because he is in difficulty. He dare not answer, and realizing the consequences of the declaration made by the minister he resorts to building up an imaginary situation. The fact still remains that the government does not know where it is going in this legislation in view of section 94A, and not knowing where it is going, as in so many cases in the past, it shuts its eye to the problem. It moves ahead ultimately toward difficulties; crises develop, and then ex parte legislation is introduced in order to meet the situation. The Prime Minister has given an answer. I accept it. They do not know where they are going.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the issue which has been raised and which is being discussed obviously is of the greatest importance to Canada. I should like to say a word or two on it, but not in terms of asking the government to say now what its policy may be if a certain thing should happen. Personally, I have the feeling that for the government to attempt to do that would not be a service to Canada or to federal relations with the provinces. To attempt to say now what may be done in circumstances, the precise nature of which are not yet known, would not be, as I have said, a service to the future of confederation in this country.
I suggest that when, in 1951, the amendment to the B.N.A. Act was made, it was obviously made because of a conviction across the country, shared by the provincial governments as well as by the federal authorities, that care of the aged of Canada must be so far as is possible equal across the country, subject to anything more that the provinces themselves may be able to do.
The principle on which this parliament has functioned in this field as I understand it, is precisely the principle that all the aged people of this country, wherever they may reside, are
Old Age Security Act Amendment entitled to at least the little we are giving them to live on for the rest of their years in some dignity and self-respect. There are parts of this country which would not be able to afford such treatment for their elders within their boundaries unless the federal parliament took action.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot accept the general and diffuse interpretation given a while ago by the right hon. Prime Minister to section 94A of the Canadian constitution, thus bestowing steadily upon the central government a responsibility in the old age security field.
Section 94A is very clear, it is one of the sections of our constitution that lends itself the least to confusion and it is to the effect that the central government cannot hinder, neither now nor in the future, the provinces that decide to exercise such authority, such constitutional responsibility.
Besides, it is consistent with the spirit and the letter of the constitution. If we take the time to read the 1865 confederation debates, we will find out easily that the fathers of confederation, the politicians of that time in Canada, wanted to leave to the provinces the whole field of social security. And the 1951 constitutional amendment implies such priority, such precedence on the part of the provinces as regards social security.
I say that an active province, which Quebec is preparing to become in this matter as stated in its speech from the throne, and which decides to occupy the old age security field has a priority right. And when its legislation is passed, well it becomes an exclusive right on its territory.
Evidently, the central government can continue to legislate and operate in the old age security field for inactive provinces which prefer to let the central government look after the matter. This is the only meaning in my opinion, which can be given to section 94A. And this is why, in view of that crucial problem which will very soon arise, probably during the winter, in Quebec city, when a provincial legislation will be passed so that the

DEBATES	December 20, 1966
Quebec government will take possession, according to its constitutional and prior responsibility, of the old age security field, it should now be foreseen what the federal government will do, if it will merely legislate in the case of other provinces, but not for the province of Quebec.
To govern is to anticipate. It is a truism we learned in college. We have had few opportunities to see it put into practice in this house since last January 18. Yes, to govern is to anticipate. And in this case, the antecedents or the precedents are what matters. When hon. members ask for a fiscal compensation, their arguments rest on antecedents, on other federal legislation where a fiscal equivalent was granted. And to quote a few examples, we have the education grants in 1964, if my memory is correct, and payments to universities in 1962. Therefore, if that procedure has given satisfaction and has abolished dissension between Canadians, between the provinces or a province and the central government, I fail to see why the present government refuses to anticipate. It is its responsibility to govern, anticipate and include in the present legislation the fiscal compensation for the provinces which will want to assume that field of social security.
The basic principle of federalism is a matter of balance and a matter of social justice also. And to reach a balance under our legislative system, it is necessary to anticipate clauses which will not result in discrimination and injustice toward any province which will want to occupy the field of social security.
If the central government refuses to anticipate, in the right direction, one can imagine what conflicts and disagreements will ensue when a province occupies the field of social security. And all this, Mr. Chairman, would occur during our centennial year, in that very year when Quebec, for instance, is going to pass within a few months, in 1967, legislation to get into the field of old age security. And the present federal government is going to let dissension occur during the centennial, when finally Canadians from coast to coast, in a fine constructive spirit, must try to prepare and cultivate further national harmony and fraternity.
I hope the government, and therefore the Minister of National Health and Welfare, will agree to amend the bill if they want it to pass rapidly and if they really want it to be free of discrimination and injustice against a province or provinces wanting to occupy the field of old age security.

Mr. Chairman, I referred to this matter first a week ago last Monday, on December 12. I did not do so because of a frivolous reason but because it is obvious, as the hon. member for York South stated, that there is a deep and serious problem here with which the government may be faced. One does not blame the government for introducing this legislation, although one may differ with the terms, but it is proceeding on the basis that in the past this field has been largely occupied by the federal government.
In view of the very definite and categorical statement by the province of Quebec, certified by the government and approved of apparently by the official opposition, it appears to be quite definite that we will shortly see provincial legislation dealing with old age security. It is not enough for the minister to say, and as the Prime Minister has said today, although there is a problem the government has a constitutional right to introduce this type of legislation. This is quite correct. I do not think anyone differs from that view. Of course, the government has the right to introduce it. But it is surely our duty, as the legislative body which authorizes the government to change the existing laws to provide for this supplement, to take a look at the future and see what will be the situation. We say to the government, here is a problem. Will you not admit it? Will you not tell us what you propose to do?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I made a suggestion, which I will come to in a minute, which I think might well be considered by the government. The hon. member for York South has raised the point. I believe that there is a very meritorious case to be made for arguing that the field is one which should properly be completely and exclusively dealt with by the federal government. I am not arguing that point now" not giving my view; there may be other opportunities to do so. But it is quite obvious that in 1951, when the then government attempted to offer that solution it was rejected by the provincial governments. We now have section 94A in its present form.
In 1964 the government, seeking the necessary constitutional amendments to permit it to introduce the Canada Pension Act, asked and secured from Westminster an amendment to section 94A providing for supplementary pensions including old age and disability. At that time I suggested the government give consideration to dealing with the provinces in an attempt to make the field exclusively federal.
Old Age Security Act Amendment Obviously, there were difficulties and impediments; the provinces no doubt did not agree. We are, therefore, faced with the situation that exists today.
I think it would be a very embarrassing, ludicrous and impossible situation if, without there being any indication of what this government intends to do, we found that the province of Quebec, or for that matter any other province, had exercised its obvious constitutional right by enacting legislation which so far as the amount, ages and conditions are concerned differed completely from the federal old age security legislation.
If you consider section 94A and its obvious, plain meaning, it would appear that the ultimate jurisdiction still lies with the provincial government. The provincial government may say: In our opinion pensions should commence at a certain age. They should be for a certain amount and should be paid under certain conditions. If this were the case, it would quite obviously not be meeting the intention indicated through their legislation with regard to limits if, in addition to the amounts they prescribe, pensioners received the amount prescribed by the federal government. It would be an impossible situation, and one with which this house must be concerned now.
The law is there. I suggested to the minister that he might give consideration to making it quite plain that the minute the province does legislate, before that legislation was actually implemented the matter would be referred to the Supreme Court. Statements, with which I do not agree, have been made in this house and outside, that this is not a matter in respect of which the Supreme Court can adjudicate. I reject that argument. On one hand, the provinces turn to the British North America Act and say, because of the way this legislation is worded we have the right to enact social security legislation. We stake our claim on the ground of the British North America Act, but reject that act when it comes to establishing the forum in which this question can be discussed and tried if there is a conflict of opinion.
That is a proposition which I cannot support. It seems to me that the government should say: There is a problem. We did not create it, but it exists. We may be coming into a situation wherein we will be met with provincial old age security legislation which differs materially from ours. Under those conditions, we recognize the problem and intend to deal with it. I think that under
11370	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment those conditions we, as a legislative body, should bring the question to the attention of the government and suggest alternative solutions. The government should recognize and accept the fact that the difficulty does exist. If we place alternatives before the government, I think we will have done all we can at this particular time.
I believe this is an important issue. It is not being raised for frivolous or delaying purposes. I think the house is entitled to raise the matter and obtain as competent and complete answers as it is possible for the government to give. I do not believe it is sufficient merely for the government to say that parliament has the right at this time to pass the legislation which the government has introduced. I agree with that position, but that is not a sufficient answer to the problem. A situation may occur in the future in this respect. I believe it is incumbent upon the government to indicate that they intend to solve the problem by negotiation and discussion, or if necessary by a reference as soon as possible to the proper forum for a final and binding adjudication. Anything less than that really does not satisfy me.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether on clause 1 I might make one or two observations about the bill itself which I think are directly related to the progress of the bill.
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, if it is not against the rules, I want to express my very deep appreciation to the hon. member for Hamilton West, who I think all members of the committee in every part of the house will agree, did a painstaking job as chairman of the committee. It has certainly not been my experience that any piece of legislation that I have had anything to do with has received a more thoroughgoing and conscientious scrutiny by a committee. I want to say that I do appreciate the part played by members from all parts of the house in their consideration of this bill.
I think we all realize that transportation, as I have said too many times already, is the bony structure of our country and that it is very important to keep the skeleton healthy if the body politic is to be at all healthy. We had a big responsibility, when we came to do something about its basic structure, to make sure that we did it well.
At the same time, I might be permitted to point out what will be the legal and administrative consequences of our failure to complete this bill by December 31. In saying this, I am not trying to kid anyone that this parliament will be able to dispose of it by December 31. I would hope this house might, but I do not think that in the few days before Christmas we could dispose of the bill in committee here and expect the hon. members of the other place to rush through a bill of this magnitude in an hour or two.
At the same time we should be aware, as I say, of the legal and administrative consequences, as nearly as I can outline them, of
December 20, 1966

our failure to pass this bill. It seems to me they illustrate the importance of making as much progress as we possibly can between now and the adjournment, so we can dispose of the measure as early as possible in the new year and offset the effects of these consequences to such extent as we can.
There is no provision in the estimates for any further payments to the railways beyond December 31 of this year. It was assumed and hoped, and I think expected until fairly recently, that this bill would have become law by that date. As these payments to the railways are to some degree made in recognition of certain things that they are doing voluntarily, it will be somewhat difficult to expect them for a long period-I hope not even for a short time; but certainly not for a long period-not to exercise what rights they may have under the law existing on January 1 unless there is evidence that we seriously intend to make changes in the law along the lines which, as a result of the deliberations of the committee, I think most of us seem disposed to make.
As hon. members know, the non-competitive freight rates have been frozen. Originally, they were frozen by law. That law has long ago expired and the rates have remained static by the voluntary action of the railways. If there is reasonable evidence to show that we are not gomg to take too long in the new year, I hope there would be no disposition on the part of the railways to disturb that freeze. But we should remember that it is not part of the law and what they are doing at the present time they are doing voluntarily.
Whatever criticisms hon. members may still have of some aspects of the new bill, I think all of us would feel that it would be very regrettable if there was any attempt to make any rate changes under the old law. We do recognize the many disadvantages that those rates have. This is particularly true in the Atlantic provinces or the select territory, which includes the eastern part of Quebec. In that area we are not merely proposing in this legislation to mainta'n the freeze for two years but we are proposing to maintain the roll-back, which would also cease to operate after December 31 unless the railways voluntarily decide to continue it in the hope that parliament will act in good faith and with reasonable expedition.

I am not critic1 zing anyone when I say this. I recognize that there has been much to do. But I feel we should know what the facts are.

The Canadian Pacific Railway has voluntarily undertaken to pay grants equal to one third of the municipal taxes which would otherwise be levied but for their constitutional exemption. They have agreed to pay these taxes in the first calendar year after the passage of this legislation. It was anticipated when this offer

was made that the year in question would be 1967. The railway will pay two thirds in the following year, and the full amount in the third year and thereafter.
This is a voluntary undertaking and while I could ask the company to overlook the fact that we have not found it possible to act by the end of December-and I would naturally be glad to do this-we must remember that this offer was made in anticipation of the freedom which would be granted under this new legislation. This freedom would enable the railways to compete for revenue in a way in which they are not able to compete at present.
Since the company is paying money out of its own treasury on the assumption that it will get this extra revenue, it would be rather humiliating for the government to have to say: notwithstanding the fact that we could not do what we had hoped and expected to do to enable you to earn these additional sums, we would nevertheless like you to pay these taxes. The government would, I think, have to reserve its decision as to whether it would impose this extra burden on the treasury-because that is what it would amount to-if parliament took too long about putting the railways in a position to earn the additional revenues which they had hoped to earn as a result of the passage of this legislation.

increases on the senior citizens. This is shameful treatment of our senior citizens. The government has used time consuming methods with respect to these three pieces of legislation, one of which is almost passed and the other two which it hopes to have passed soon.
I honestly believe that the Minister of Transport did his best to get this bill through the house by January 1. I hold nothing against him, except I am sorry he did not have more persuasive power with his colleagues. He should have been able to convince them that this legislation should have been introduced sooner because consideration of it would require more time than is available between now and January 1 next.
I want to point out that we on this side of the chamber co-operated fully when the legislation was introduced. We gave up the resolution stage debate, which could have lasted ten days on such an important piece of legislation. We gracefully acknowledged the fact that there was only so much time left for consideration of the bill, and then we proceeded as quickly as possible to give the bill first and second reading and send it to the transport committee.
In the transport committee we heard one brief after another in rapid succession. I do not hold this against the minister, the government or the committee chairman, but we heard the briefs in rapid succession. In the process 3,000 pages of evidence were piled up, in an endeavour to return the bill to the house as soon as possible so that it could be dealt with by January 1, 1967. If it is not now dealt with by that date I say the responsibility lies with the government, and not with the minister or with the opposition. Both the minister and the committee worked to meet the time objective, but we were unable to convince the minister's colleagues that they should co-operate.
This is an important piece of legislation, and I am going to quote the minister's exact words, as recorded at page 1666 of volume 23 of the standing committee's proceedings, to show hon. members what we are dealing with here. The minister said:
There is not, I am sure, any more important piece of legislation before parliament, not even the Bank Act, which I do not wish to disparage in any way but which is, after all, just a revision of existing legislation.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Then the minister went on to say:
This is a fundamentally revolutionary change that is being proposed here.

December 20, 1966
Transportation
This is not in an ordinary thing; this is a fundamental, revolutionary change which is being presented in this bill. In the light of this, I urge the committee to consider this bill very fully. Then, he went on to say:
We are proposing for the first time since 1903, when the board of railway commissioners was first established and rates were set for practically all kinds of railway activity, to put the railways in a position of running themselves like any other business does except in the areas where they have a monopoly.
In other words, after this bill is passed, the railroads will be like any other business, except in areas where they have a monopoly. That has been the contentious issue. Where are those areas, and what protection does this bill give those areas?
Then at the top of page 1667 he went on to explain what a difficult time he had in attempting to agree with this revolutionary change. He said that it was difficult to come to such an agreement. He dealt at quite some length with the difficulty which he had in wrestling with this whole problem. So, this bill is put before us. It contains a revolutionary change, a departure. In the committee on transport and communications, we were asked to consider this at length.
I should like to touch a little on the history of transportation in Canada. The Manitoba brief, in proceedings and evidence No. 38, dealt with this question. I should like to read from page 2555 of the committee proceedings:
In the early days of confederation, national policy was concentrated mainly on fostering the political unity and economic integration of the newly united provinces.
In other words, transportation played a real part in bringing us together politically and economically. Now, this policy is going to be discarded in this new bill. We are going to treat the transportation system as just another business. That is the first real step we are taking in clause 1 of the bill. The submission continues:
Due to the distances which separate Canada's producing territories and consumer markets, development of the country's resources depended upon railway construction and low transportation charges to facilitate the flow of products to market. The people of Canada have given the aid necessary to procure adequate transportation facilities.
In other words, down through the years, through taxation the people of Canada have provided adequate transportation facilities to enable the producing areas to get their goods to market and the consuming areas to utilize 
the goods produced all across Canada. The submission continues:
The ultimate goal of the public policies of the various federal governments since confederation was to maximize and equalize opportunities and benefits for all Canadians in all regions of the country.
That has been the basic reasoning behind all transportation policies in years gone by. This bill is a revolutionary change from all that. It will set up the railroads as business entities and the suggestion is that we no longer need them as public utilities. In a sense, this is what we are being told; this is what this bill purports to do. Let us look at the possibilities. Are they still public utilities? Are they something similar to General Motors, or are they something similar to a Canadian utility which is providing power, for example, to the city of Ottawa, or something like that? According to my interpretation they certainly still are to quite a large extent public utilities.
One has only to go through the committee proceedings. One might look at page 1669 of committee proceedings No. 23 where it is outlined clearly by the minister that these rates are going to be subsidized. These are subsidized rates for grain moving to the maritime ports. In other words, there is an area here in which the railway still is a public utility. We see in the bill, as the minister points out on this same page, that the Crowsnest pass rates will be maintained at a subsidized rate, and in a sense the railways still are a public utility.
One could go through the areas of Canada and point out the many aspects in which the transportation system in Canada is still basically a public utility. Even if it is only partially so, then government regulations should have something to do with the permissible earnings of that public utility. If the government is going to give somebody a sole right to serve a given area, then it is its duty to make sure that the level of rates charged in that area are not exorbitant or abusive. If one feels they are not a public utility but rather a corporate entity, then of course there is nothing to stop them going ahead and charging any rates they wish.
One other aspect with which I should like to deal is that clause 1, in a sense sets up, the commission and does so in such a way that it causes some concern to the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. The commission is not necessarily going to be a cure-all. Just because we link all modes of transportation under one commission does not necessarily mean we are solving
December 20, 1966

all our transportation problems. This is outlined very well by the C.P.R. in committee proceedings No. 28 at page 2059. The C.P.R. had this to say about the establishment of the commission itself:
The McPherson Commission did not contemplate a commission having jurisdiction over all modes of transport.
Many people believe that this piece of legislation is based directly on the MacPherson Commission report, but here the C.P.R. points out that the MacPherson Commission did not envisage a commission such as this bill would set up to have jurisdiction over all modes of transportation. It recommended the creation of a national transportation advisory council to undertake the task of conducting the studies necessary to achieve the goals of a national transportation policy. They go on to deal at some length with what a national transportation policy should include. They say this:
It is important that care be taken that the study and research function of the commission does not become confused with its regulatory function, nor that it results in the commission assuming some of the functions of management.
In other words, a warning is given. The MacPherson Commission did not necessarily recommend a commission which would be as all encompassing as this one is.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Mr. MacDougall also suggested the MacPherson Commission felt that care should be taken to make sure that the research and administrative functions of the commission were not to be too closely knit or related to the regulatory functions of management. As recorded at page 1728 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the committee on transport and communications a representative of the C.N.R. said:
Well, the new national transportation legislation that they have in the United States in so far as the regulation of railroads is concerned, is mainly directed to the general sort of administrative and research aspects. They have not attempted by that to take over into this new body the functions of the Interstate Commerce Commission in regulating and controlling various modes of transport.
In other words, in the United States the national transportation policy is related to administrative and research aspects while the Interstate Commerce Commission is the regulatory and controlling body. Through this bill we are trying to link these together. At the same page Mr. MacDougall of the C.N.R. dealt at some length with the dangers involved in linking these several functions.
Transportation
At pages 1768 and 1769 Dr. Bandeen pointed out that the research aspect must be kept independent. He said:
First of all, we have a feeling that there is a need for independent research-independent of the government, independent of industry in Canada-
He wondered whether or not this independent research would really remain independent over the years if it were linked closely with a regulatory body. There is a danger in this regard. Caution should be taken in setting up this commission to see that all modes of transportation are not placed under its jurisdiction. The two briefs presented to the commission which dealt to any extent at all with commodity pipe lines suggested that their operations should not fall under the jurisdiction of a commission such as will be set up by this bill, and that they might better be left under the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board. I think we are going too fast by placing regulatory and research functions in the same category, and by placing all modes of transportation under one commission. That is not a recommendation of the MacPherson Commission. Representatives of the railroads themselves have expressed fear about putting regulatory and research aspects under one commission.
I should like to mention one other aspect of this bill to which the minister has referred, and I have in mind the formula devised for rail line abandonments. Some years ago 4,000 miles of railroad trackage on the three prairie provinces were the subject of abandonment applications. If my memory serves me correctly, 1,800 miles of trackage on the three prairie provinces is to be abandoned. That is nearly half the trackage involved in the prairie provinces. In this regard, I intend to move an amendment to clause 1 of this bill which I hope the minister will consider seriously. It is my proposal that the word "adequate" should be added to line 4 of the first page of the bill. In other words, it now reads:
It is hereby declared that an economic and efficient transportation system_
I suggest the word "adequate" should be added so that it would read:
It is hereby declared that an adequate, economic and efficient transportation system-
That may appear to be unimportant, but I suggest it means a great deal when you consider the wording of that clause and the attitude of representatives of railway companies, particularly in areas of the prairie provinces. What is the most economic and efficient transportation system? Perhaps one track running

Transportation
through the heart of the prairies would be the most economic and efficient, but that is taking efficiency and economics to the 'nth degree. This clause does not take into consideration the adequacy of the system, as was suggested by the Manitoba brief.
Let me deal now with this general rail line abandonment aspect of a transportation system. On the prairies, we are very concerned about these abandonments because when the minister made his announcement regarding this bill there were 4,000 miles of track proposed for abandonment. The minister announced that 1,800 miles of the 4,000 miles involved in applications for abandonment had been nailed down to protect certain areas. He said the other 2,200 miles-

The minister stated clearly in the house last Friday that these applications would not be proceeded with until the bill before us was passed. I should like to be clear on that point, because when this bill is passed presumably these applications will be dealt with by the new commission. I should like this difficulty cleared up before we pass clause 1 of this bill. If 2,200 miles of trackage on the prairies is to be nailed down, the citizens of the areas involved should know why one track is to be maintained until 1970 whereas another will be abandoned. In other words, in order that various lines be treated on an equal basis they should all be considered under this new transportation concept. I have some doubts in this regard as to clause 89.

My interpretation of this new concept is that applications now before the Board of Transport Commissioners will be dealt with after this bill is passed and the new commission is set up. What I should like to know is whether the Board of Transport Commissioners will then deal with the applications now in existence. That is what the railroads think. This is the reason 1 am raising the question of rail line abandonment. If some lines are to be saved under this new transportation concept, the commission should judge other lines in the same light. I cannot stress this point too strongly because there is, without doubt, a great deal of concern across the country in this respect.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I should like to deal with one other matter under clause 1 of the bill. What does this measure do? We are setting up a commission to regulate all modes of transportation. We are going to remove, to some extent, the regulations that now govern and control the railroads. We are going to free the railroads. What will be the end result of this measure? I have come to the conclusion, after sitting in the committee for many, many days and asking numerous questions, that the end result will be increased freight rates. One has only to read pages 1765 and 1766 of the committee proceedings te come to this conclusion.
As will be seen from page 1765 of the committee proceedings, Mr. Gordon was asked this question, and Mr. MacMillan was asked questions in this connection at the top of page 1766. The answer given was that there was no alternative, freight rates would be increased. The hon. member for Wellington-Huron prodded the president and future president of the C.N.R. The answer was that freight rates would be going up. The question was asked in Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 28, as will be found at pages 1970 to 1972. It was asked of Mr. Crump, chairman of the C.P.R., and he said that after careful consideration freight rates would go up. They have to go up because the subsidies are being reduced and the railroads have been subjected to a freight rate freeze. Everything has been going up.
The result of this bill will be an increase in freight rates. Let us consider that aspect of the matter alone and ask ourselves whether we should hurriedly pass this bill. Inflation has run rampant across Canada in the past year. It is now slowing up a little. What effect will the passage of this bill have on the economy? Transportation has a bearing on the cost of everything we consume and produce. The
December 20, 1966

presidents of the two major railroads have said that if this bill passes, freight rates will go up. The price of goods will therefore go up; there is no alternative. Any increase in freight rates will be passed on to the consumer in Canada or some other country. We are going to increase inflationary pressures with the passage of this bill. There is no other conclusion to which one can come after reading those pages of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the committee to which I referred.
The consumer will pay a higher price for goods because the cost of transportation is a built-in cost in respect of everything we produce and consume in Canada. This is another matter that we, as legislators, should consider very, very carefully at this time. We have seen inflation run rampant across Canada. Housewives from Vancouver to Halifax have become organized and have been boycotting supermarkets to an extent never before envisaged in this country. Certain measures have attempted to deal with the problem of inflation. I refer to the attempted budget of a couple of months ago, and the budget of last night. These measures attempted to deal with the problem of inflation. I believe that inflation is reaching the end of its course, and that the passage of this bill will result in more fuel being thrown on the fire of inflation. Once again, prices will spiral.

This is very generous of the committee, Mr. Chairman, and I will not abuse the generosity of hon. members by continuing at length. I have said what I think this bill will do. It is an all-encompassing bill. It sets up a commission to look into the problems of transportation. In summary, I would say I am gravely concerned about this commission. I wonder whether it will have the proper facilities to undertake research and look into the regulatory and management aspects of transportation. A real attempt, should be made by the commission and the government to keep these two aspects as separate as
Transportation
possible. The whole country, particularly western Canada, wants an answer to the question I have raised with regard to rail line abandonment. Will the applications now before the commission be dealt with by the commission after this bill passes, or will they be dealt with by the old Board of Transport Commissioners? This is a question to which many, many people in western Canada would like an answer. They are very concerned about this matter.
The people of western Canada see some rail lines being saved under our new transportation policy, and some discarded. In a sense that is just what they are, discarded. There is some hope held out for some lines until 1975, and no hope for others. These people want to know the formula which provides this degree of safety for some lines but not others. That formula was never given in committee. There was an attempt at rationalization on this question. An hon. member asked whether the criterion used was so many thousand bushels a day to be hauled per mile of track. The minister said no, we could not really peg it on that. He said that criterion was used, but we could not peg it on that sort of thing.
The question of rail line abandonment is extremely important. Of course, the most important aspect of this whole transporation legislation is this: We as legislators, must ask ourselves whether we consider the railroads in Canada to be corporate entities with no obligation other than to make a profit for their shareholders, or do we consider them still to be providing a public service and to be partially, if not completely, public utilities? This is the question we must ask ourselves before this bill passes or even before too many clauses are dealt with. When we reach clause 16, say, we will have to decide whether we consider railroads to be 50 per cent or 60 per cent public utilities. We will have to direct our remarks to this aspect of the matter and decide whether clause 16 will give the protection necessary in order that the shippers and citizens of this country may utilize the public utilities which we have set up and enjoyed over the years.
In concluding my remarks on clause 1, Mr. Chairman, I point out that I will be moving an amendment to this clause. I will not do so at this time because it would be fairer if the minister had an opportunity to consider my suggestion. The suggestion is to include the word "adequate" in the clause. I hope the minister, his officials and the government, will consider the inclusion of that word because I

December 20, 1966
Transportation
believe it should be in the clause. I think that all people in this country, particulary those in the west, believe we must have an adequate, economic and efficient transportation system.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
This was suggested in the brief submitted by the Manitoba government.
I will conclude my remarks with the suggestion that if the bill is passed at this time-even if it is passed by December 31 as the minister urges that it should be-we will be adding fuel to the inflationary fires because the costs of transportation will go up. 1 believe that this point should be considered during the debate on the bill. We should remember that inflation has been one of the greatest problems which has faced Canada during the past year.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the preamble to the bill advises us that the bill is intended to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada. In the minister's own words the intent of the bill is to bring about a fundamental change in our transportation policy, in the freight rate charges, etc. This being so, I think the minister was quite right in pointing out a little earlier that he really does not expect us on this side of the house to hurry along the passage of this legislation. It is unfortunate if the delay in processing this legislation will cause some embarrassment to the government. However, this problem will have to lie on their doorstep because it is the result of their own actions. When the minister spoke about the awkwardness which will result from the delay in the passage of the legislation he must have realized that he will simply have to find ways and means of extricating the government from this awkward position. He mentioned the fact that certain orders in council will lapse at the end of the year. I suggest that if it is only a case of orders in council lapsing, the cabinet will have to deal with that problem as they see fit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Unfortunately, it is not only orders in council which will lapse but also statutes.

speechtext:
In that case, I expect that the railway companies and the government will be able to come to some understanding so that the spirit and intent of the new legislation will be honoured in the interval until it actually comes into effect.
I wish to take this opportunity to make some remarks on the over-all purpose and

intent of the legislation. It seems to me that in putting forward the legislation the government and the minister have committed one rather obvious error. They have taken the railway transportation and freight charges further away from regulation and have put too much faith in competition as an effective means of protecting the public interest. It may well be that certain evidence has come to light in the past years which would indicate that competition has increased in recent years, and has thereby become more effective in protecting the users of transportation services. That premise is certainly open to debate. But even if it were to be conceded that in some respects competition in the transportation industry has increased, it is also a fact that in certain regions of this country this is less true.
I think that those regions of this country which produce primary products will be adversely affected by the provisions of this legislation when it becomes law. I submit that there has not been sufficient evidence put forward to date to indicate that we would be well advised to consider competition as a proper basis for the control of freight charges in this country. I believe the hon. member for Acadia was right when he said that it is in the national interest to continue regarding railway transportation as a public utility. I think he said this on several occasions. If it is, in fact, to be considered as a public utility then we should continue to rely upon regulation as the proper means of protecting the public interest.
However, I wish to give the minister credit for the fact that, after having introduced the bill and having sat in the committee where representations were made by various organizations, he acknowledged some errors in the legislation. In fact, he proposed a large number of amendments to the bill.
I have made a rough estimate of the amendments which have already been incorporated into the revised version of the bill and they number around 60 or 64. The net effect of the more important aspects of these amendments was for the government to retreat a little way toward a greater reliance on regulation as a means of protecting the public interest. I think the minister, after having heard the numerous submissions made to the committee, realized that too many people were concerned and worried by the tendency of the legislation to emphasize competition rather than regulation. After this was pointed out to the minister, he acquiesced to a certain extent and put forward some amendments to the bill.
December 20, 1966

Even if we acknowledge at this stage that we should rely on regulation more rather than less, it must also be said that if regulation is to prove effective it must be given a chance. By this I mean that the commission, which is the regulating authority, must be given proper terms of reference and proper statutory authority to do its job. However, what do we have in the bill? The most important clauses of the bill having to do with rate control and regulation contain terms of reference and formulae which are not based on reality but on some fictitious standards.
Almost every organization which appeared before the committee and presented briefs has objected vociferously to those standards which, nevertheless, have been allowed to remain in the bill as originally drafted. I wish to say to the minister that, owing to the fact these important objections have not been dealt with and the right kind of changes were not made in this respect, I and several other hon. members here would find it very difficult to vote in the affirmative on these clauses. Of course, it follows that we would find it difficult to vote in the affirmative on the entire bill.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I do not want to take time at this stage to enter into any kind of polemic debate or digression as to the desirability for or relative effectiveness of public ownership versus private ownership in our transportation policy. But it seems to me that if we are to be really serious about defining and implementing a national transportation policy that is rational to the highest possible degree, we must enter upon such a debate, and the sooner the better.
There may be no virtue in public ownership in itself. I submit there is no virtue in private ownership in itself where there exists the kind of circumstances which require pervasive regulation in order to protect the public interest. Yet, that is precisely what we must have; we must have pervasive regulation of our transportation services in order to protect the public interest.
As I have already said, the reason for that is that there is simply not enough evidence to date to show conclusively that we can move toward more and more reliance upon competition as the means of protecting those who use our transportation services in order to stimulate their functions in our economy.
As a member of the standing committee on transportation and communications which was charged with the responsibility of studying
Transportation
this bill clause by clause, may I say I found the experience very worth while. In many ways I felt we did accomplish something. But in one very important respect the work of the committee was an exercise in futility. I refer specifically to the fact that the committee really could not make a proper and definitive evaluation of this bill and its likely effects unless it were provided with certain necessary and crucial cost accounting data which was in the possession of the railway companies.
On one occasion the hon. member for Medicine Hat and myself moved a motion asking that the committee be given precisely this information. Without it, it was simply impossible to arrive at any conclusion as to the efficacy of the proposed section 336 having to do with rate control. The rate control which is referred to in that clause has to do with costs incurred by the railways and the formulas which are based on costs incurred by the railways. The committee could not get this data that related to costs.
My motion was defeated, Mr. Chairman. At that point I did give notice that I would raise in the house, as I am now, this grievance, and I believe it is a real grievance. I contend that the committee was foiled and frustrated in its task by being refused cost data in the possession of the railways.
The ostensible reason given was that this information was part of the proprietary rights of Canadian companies. While the information could be given to the transportation commission, it could not be given to any other group, including a committee of this parliament, because it might break some kind of confidence and put the railways at a disadvantage in relation to their competitors.
I submit that this kind of argument is completely unacceptable. It would not be accepted by any legislative committee of the United States Congress or, I submit, of the British parliament. I might add that the submissions made by the three prairie provinces were to the effect they considered it unfortunate that this information was not provided to the counsel for the three prairie provinces. They mentioned specifically that it was unfortunate this data was not made available to the members of the parliamentary standing committee.
So I must say, Mr. Chairman, that no member in this committee, with the possible exception of the Minister of Transport, can say with any degree of confidence or assurance that he really comprehends the impact of certain proposed sections in this bill, particularly

December 20, 1986
Transportation
section 336 and one or two others. He has never been provided with certain data which would have enabled him to evaluate the effect of those sections. Parliament should be apprised of these facts. In a sense, Mr. Chairman, we are being asked to pass upon legislation the effect of some of the clauses of which is a matter of mystery, doubt and uncertainty. I am wondering whether parliament likes to be put in the position of passing legislation on that basis.
I wish to advise the minister that during the course of the clause by clause consideration of this bill I will have a number of amendments to propose. I propose to move them in such a way as to facilitate discussion, to give the minister an opportunity to indicate why they should or should not be accepted, and then we can move on. I certainly agree it is important at this stage to put this legislation through as quickly as is prudently possible, even though in major respects we find this bill to be based on faulty premises and questionable grounds.
We shall certainly expect from the minister further elaboration and clarification-because he is in a better position to do so than other members here-as to the likely effect of this bill particularly on western Canada and those regions of the country which are primary producing. According to my understanding of the bill and of the formulae contained in it, it would seem to militate against those very regions which produce what might be called heavy loading commodities, bulk commodities

in short, for want of a better term, primary products.
There are, of course, safeguards in the bill with respect to grain and so on. But what about, for example, regions in northwestern and northern Ontario which are dependent upon shipments of lumber and forest products? What about shipments of natural resources in their raw state? How will these areas be affected? It is my opinion that they will be affected adversely by this legislation.
May I also point out to hon. members that in the submissions made by some rather learned men in the fields of transportation regulation and transportation economics, much the same kind of statement was made to the listener or inference left to the reader, namely that it is these I have mentioned that will be at a disadvantage following the passage of this legislation.
If I may make this suggestion to the minister, I would say that the proper basis for
[Mr. Schreyer.l
regulation, whether of transportation of utilities of another kind, is permitted earnings, fair returns and allied concepts. I know the minister does not think much of this basis for regulation bacause I have heard him say, in jocular fashion during the hearings of the committee, that the idea of a fair return is a medieval notion.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Yet, that is precisely the basis which most of our public utility regulatory bodies use. What other basis can there be? Fictitious formulae, that is all we have in this bill. The idea of a fair return, a permitted level of earnings, is one which has been put forward by the province of Manitoba and by the counsel for the province of Alberta. I do not know whether they have been converted to the politics of social democracy. Nevertheless, they have advocated this basis as a foundation for a regulation in the transportation field.
I do not think there is anything medieval about a notion of this kind. I think it is timeless. I think it has existed in the minds of men for ages, and that it will continue to exist even though it seems to have departed from the minds of some hon. members, who in many other ways are very fine gentlemen but who do not appear to be impressed by such a valid and attainable idea as regulation based on the notion of a fair return.
Before resuming my seat, I want to ask the minister whether he would not take a minute or two for the purpose of elaborating what he had to say earlier about the intention with respect to applications for branch line abandonment. I know that in the past two or three days the minister has been questioned in the house regarding an application which is said to have been sent to the Board of Transport Commissioners by the Canadian Pacific Railway requesting the abandonment of a particular branch line.
The impression I have is that the minister gave an assurance some time ago that all applications for abandonment would be withdrawn, and would not be entertained until this legislation becomes effective. How, then, does he explain the fact, if it is a fact, that the C.P.R. has made an application for abandonment in the course of the past few days? I believe the minister said earlier today that the board would not consider applications. It is my understanding that the board will not even accept applications until this legislation becomes effective.

The situation is this: The hon. member for Acadia said there were four thousand miles of line-I have not checked the figure myself, but I have no doubt he is right, or approximately right-which have been the subject of applications before the board for a number of years. The railways have agreed not to proceed with these applications.
Then, one day last September I think it was, the government issued a statement and published a map showing the lines on which no abandonment would be permitted to take place before January 1, 1975, if this legislation passed. We could not give any kind of guarantee as to what would happen if it did not pass, because the law is the law. But we said it would be part of the policy of which this legislation is another part, that these lines would be protected, and if the railways were losing money on them they could in due course under this legislation get a subsidy.
As for the rest of the applications affecting the other 1,800 miles of line, the applications had already been made. To the best of my knowledge no new applications of any kind have been made. Both railway companies wrote to the board indicating that they intended to abandon all their applications affecting the protected lines on the day this legislation received royal assent, and asking the board to take note of this fact. The board undoubtedly did so.
Whether on the initiative of the railways, particularly the C.P.R., or on its own, the board began to gather information about the other lines so that whenever the time came for hearings to be held, those hearings could go forward and the necessary up-to-date statistical information would be available. The board is a court of record, as hon. members
Transportation
know. It does not report to me what it does, as a court. I did not know that this information was being gathered-I say th.s quite frankly-until the matter was brought to my attention, first by a telegram from the Manitoba Branch Line Association and then by hon. members in this house. I inquired promptly about it, and I was assured there was no thought whatever of holding any hearings or dealing with these applications as long as the legislation was before the house. All that was being done was a certain amount of housekeeping, and I have a formal assurance to this effect from the chairman of the board.
The other question which has been raised by the hon. member for Acadia and by the hon. member for Springfield-I am sure it will also be raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat-is whether, if and when this legislation is passed, the protection of the legislation with respect to branch lines will be brought into effect immediately so that all the hearings and applications will be under the new rules, or whether the old rules will still apply. This is a question which, I believe, is not resolved one way or the other in the bill. When we come to our study of the particular clauses I will be glad to make a more detailed statement. One would have to pay some attention to the fact that it is always wrong to assume that a piece of legislation is ever going to pass. It is, therefore, a little difficult to answer this question right now.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I am aware of it, but one factor will depend upon how long it is before we can expect the legislation to pass. However, I shall be prepared to give a categorical answer to the question when we reach clause 89. I think I have explained what the situation is now. So long as this legislation is before parliament and has not received royal assent, the chairman of the board has assured me no hearings whatsoever will take place on any of the applications, some of which have been before the board for years. I think that is the essential thing for the moment.
